title.en: Onset of the Little Ice Age

lead.en: Glaciers advance and Greenland's Viking farms fade

summary.en: By one dating, a long cooling began in the Northern Hemisphere around 1300: Alpine glaciers advanced and Norse Greenland declined. Its limits are debated, and many scientists start the period in the 15th or 16th century.

title.en: Golden age of Kilwa and the Swahili coast

lead.en: Gold and ivory tie East Africa to Arabia, India and China

summary.en: The Muslim trading towns of the East African coast, among them Kilwa, Mombasa, Malindi and Zanzibar, shipped Zimbabwean gold and ivory to Arabia, India and China. Kilwa minted its own coins and built stone mosques and palaces such as Husuni Kubwa.

lead.en: Yoruba portrait bronzes that astonished 20th-century Europe

summary.en: In the 12th–15th centuries the artists of Ile-Ife, the sacred city of the Yoruba, cast in copper alloys and modelled in terracotta strikingly naturalistic heads of rulers. Ife was one of the largest cities of 14th-century West Africa. A find of 1938 overturned the European belief that such art could not have arisen in Africa.

lead.en: An Ilkhanid vizier writes the first history of the world

summary.en: Rashid al-Din, vizier of the Ilkhanate, compiled for Ghazan and Öljaitü a vast history of the Mongols, Turks, Chinese, Indians, Jews and 'Franks', often called the first world history. Illustrated copies were produced in workshops in Tabriz. It is the main source on Genghis Khan and his descendants.

lead.en: For nearly 70 years the popes live under the French king's wing

summary.en: In 1309 Pope Clement V moved his residence to Avignon, placing the papacy under strong French influence. The popes returned to Rome only in 1377, shortly before the Western Schism.

title.en: Abu Bakr II sails into the Atlantic

lead.en: A Mali ruler is said to have sailed west and never returned

summary.en: Mansa Musa said his predecessor sent a fleet to find the far edge of the ocean; when only one ship returned, he led thousands of boats west himself. He never came back, and the throne passed to Musa.

lead.en: The cathedral that took the height record from the Great Pyramid

summary.en: Around 1311 a spire some 160 m tall was raised on the central tower of Lincoln Cathedral. It was the first structure in millennia to top the Great Pyramid, and it stood until a storm brought it down in 1548.

lead.en: Three years of rain rot the harvest across northern Europe

summary.en: In spring 1315 relentless rains began across Northern Europe, rotting crops three years running. An estimated 5–12% of people died; in Flemish Ypres alone one in ten perished, three decades before the Black Death.

title.en: The Kebra Nagast, 'Glory of the Kings'

lead.en: The Queen of Sheba, the Ark and the right of Ethiopia's kings

summary.en: In the early 14th century the Glory of the Kings was compiled in Ethiopia in the Ge'ez language. It tells how the Queen of Sheba bore Solomon a son, Menelik, who brought the Ark of the Covenant to Aksum. The legend upheld the claims of the Solomonic dynasty, which ruled Ethiopia until 1974.

lead.en: Chroniclers say his gold sank its value in Cairo

summary.en: Mali's ruler Mansa Musa made the pilgrimage to Mecca with a vast retinue and caravan of gold; chroniclers say his largesse in Cairo depressed the price of gold for years. Back home he built the Djinguereber Mosque, making Timbuktu a centre of learning.

lead.en: Legend says an eagle on a cactus marked the spot

summary.en: According to legend, the Mexica Aztecs founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco where they saw an eagle perched on a cactus. The city of causeways and canals became the Aztec capital and one of the world's largest cities; Mexico City stands on its site.

lead.en: Nearly 30 years on the road, from Mali to China

summary.en: The Moroccan Ibn Battuta left his native Tangier on pilgrimage and spent nearly 30 years travelling. He journeyed from Mali and East Africa to India and China, covering an estimated 120,000 kilometres.

title.en: Ivan Kalita becomes Prince of Moscow

lead.en: Backed by the Horde and the Church, Moscow begins its rise

summary.en: In 1325 Ivan Kalita became Prince of Moscow, and Metropolitan Peter moved his seat to the city. Gaining the Horde's patent for the grand princely title and the right to collect tribute, Ivan I laid the basis of Moscow's rise.

lead.en: Nearly 500 killed at a fortified village on the Missouri

summary.en: Around 1325 a fortified farming village on the Missouri was stormed, and almost all its people, some 500, were killed. Their remains were found in a ditch in 1978; the bones show signs of scalping and malnutrition. It is one of the grimmest pieces of evidence for warfare in pre-Columbian North America.

lead.en: Modena fights Bologna, and the winner takes a bucket

summary.en: In 1325 Modena routed a Bolognese army several times its size at Zappolino, one of the largest battles of medieval Italy. The trophy was a wooden bucket taken from a Bologna well; legend says the war started over it.

lead.en: A long blockade gives the Ottomans their first capital

summary.en: After a blockade lasting years, Byzantine Prusa surrendered to Orhan, son of Osman. It became the first capital of the Ottoman state, and Osman and Orhan were buried there. Three decades later the Ottomans crossed into Europe and moved their capital to Edirne.

lead.en: A mud masterpiece that townsfolk re-plaster every year

summary.en: Returning from his pilgrimage to Mecca, Mansa Musa brought back the Andalusian poet and architect al-Sahili. Around 1327 he built a great mud-brick mosque in Timbuktu, reportedly for 200 kg of gold. Djinguereber became the emblem of a city of scholars and manuscripts. Its earthen walls are still re-plastered by the whole town every year, and it has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1988.

lead.en: Tver kills a Horde envoy, and Moscow helps the Horde punish it

summary.en: The people of Tver killed the Horde envoy Chol Khan, a cousin of Khan Özbeg, and his troops. The khan sent a punitive army, joined by Ivan Kalita of Moscow, and the principality of Tver was laid waste. Moscow received the patent for the grand principality and overtook its main rival.

lead.en: South India gains one of the world's richest capitals

summary.en: The brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty founded the Vijayanagara Empire in southern India. Its capital on the Tungabhadra (modern Hampi) became one of the world's richest cities, and the empire held off the Deccan sultanates for two centuries.

lead.en: A fight over France's throne forges two nations

summary.en: The Plantagenet kings of England contested the French throne with the Valois in a war that ran, with truces, for 116 years. Despite English victories at Crécy, Poitiers and Agincourt, France eventually recovered nearly all its land, and both nations emerged with a stronger national identity.

title.en: Sergius of Radonezh founds his monastery

lead.en: A forest hermitage becomes Moscow's spiritual centre

summary.en: Around 1337 Sergius of Radonezh built a small wooden Trinity church in the forest. His community grew into the largest monastery in Rus', and tradition says Sergius blessed Dmitry Donskoy before the Battle of Kulikovo. The Trinity Lavra is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

lead.en: Plague kills a third to half of Europe's people

summary.en: Genoese galleys from Caffa brought plague to Messina in Sicily, from where it swept across Europe. Within a few years the Black Death killed an estimated third to half of the continent's population, reshaping its economy and society.

lead.en: England's highest order of chivalry is named after a garter

summary.en: Edward III founded the order around 1348. Legend says a lady dropped her garter at a ball; the king tied it round his own leg, saying "Shame on him who thinks evil of it", which became the order's motto.

lead.en: Siam gains a capital and a kingdom for four centuries

summary.en: By the traditional date, in 1351 (or 1350 by other reckonings) the ruler U Thong, who took the name Ramathibodi I, founded a city on an island where the Chao Phraya, Pa Sak and Lopburi rivers meet. Ayutthaya absorbed Sukhothai, sacked Angkor and traded with China, Japan, Persia and Europe; by the 17th century it was one of Asia's largest cities. The Burmese destroyed it in 1767.

lead.en: Thirty against thirty: a fight by appointment mid-war

summary.en: In the middle of the Hundred Years' War, the captains of two Breton castles agreed to settle their quarrel with a fight of 30 knights against 30, like a tournament. It lasted all day, with a break for rest and drink; the French side won.

lead.en: Fa Ngum unites the 'Land of a Million Elephants', future Laos

summary.en: Fa Ngum, a Lao prince raised at the Khmer court, united the principalities of the Mekong with a Khmer army and in 1353 proclaimed the kingdom of Lan Xang, 'a Million Elephants'. Its capital, Muang Sua, was later renamed Luang Prabang after the sacred Phra Bang Buddha. In 1707 the kingdom split into three.

lead.en: A storm breaks the dikes and drowns the town of Rungholt

summary.en: On 16 January 1362 a North Sea storm broke dykes from England to Denmark, drowning an estimated 25,000 people or more. The trading town of Rungholt vanished beneath the waves and became the legend of a 'northern Atlantis'.

lead.en: Lithuania wins Kiev and the Dnieper lands from the Horde

summary.en: Grand Duke Algirdas of Lithuania defeated the armies of three Horde beys. Kiev and vast southern lands passed to Lithuania. From then on, the former Kievan Rus' was divided between two centres, Moscow and Vilnius.

lead.en: Mongols expelled — a native dynasty rules China again

summary.en: Rebel leader Zhu Yuanzhang drove out the Mongols and proclaimed the Ming dynasty with its capital at Nanjing. The Ming ruled China for nearly three centuries, rebuilding the Great Wall and raising the Forbidden City in Beijing.

lead.en: Conquests from Delhi to Anatolia adorn a new capital

summary.en: Timur (Tamerlane) seized power in Transoxiana and made Samarkand the capital of his empire. His campaigns devastated lands from Delhi to Anatolia, while craftsmen were brought to Samarkand to build its mosques and madrasas.

title.en: Stephen of Perm creates the Old Permic alphabet

lead.en: An alphabet so the Komi could worship in their own tongue

summary.en: Around 1372 the monk Stephen, later Bishop of Perm, devised an alphabet for the Komi language from Greek and Cyrillic letters and local clan marks. Service books were translated into it, and the Komi were baptised in their own language. It is one of the oldest scripts of any Finno-Ugric people.

lead.en: Crowds dance for weeks in the towns of the Rhineland

summary.en: In the summer of 1374 people in Aachen, then Cologne, Metz and other towns, began dancing nonstop until they collapsed. The cause is still unknown; suggestions range from mass hysteria to ergot poisoning.

lead.en: How dynasties rise and fall: a forerunner of sociology

summary.en: Taking refuge in a fortress on the edge of the desert, the Tunisian historian Ibn Khaldun wrote the Introduction to his world history. In it he explained how group solidarity (asabiyya) brings nomads to power and city life wears it away, so that dynasties turn over in three or four generations. He is seen as a forerunner of sociology and economics.

title.en: Jikji, printed with movable metal type

lead.en: Movable metal type nearly 80 years before Gutenberg

summary.en: In 1377 the Heungdeok temple in Cheongju printed 'Jikji', a collection of Buddhist teachings, using movable metal type. It is the oldest surviving book printed this way, nearly 80 years older than the Gutenberg Bible. Only the second volume survives, held by the National Library of France in Paris, and Korea has long sought its return.

lead.en: Moscow's first big victory over a Horde army in open battle

summary.en: The army of Dmitry of Moscow routed a Horde force under Begich, sent by the warlord Mamai, on the Vozha. It was the first major victory of the Russian princes over the Horde in open battle. Mamai retaliated by ravaging Ryazan, and two years later marched on Rus' himself, to Kulikovo Field.

lead.en: Rus' wins its first major victory over the Horde

summary.en: Forces of the Russian principalities led by Grand Prince Dmitry of Moscow defeated the army of the Horde warlord Mamai. The victory raised Moscow's standing as the centre for uniting the Russian lands and earned Dmitry the name Donskoy.

lead.en: Two years after Kulikovo, the Horde's tribute returns

summary.en: Khan Tokhtamysh suddenly appeared before Moscow while Dmitry Donskoy was raising troops in the north. The citizens held out for three days, using firearms for the first time, but opened the gates on false promises, and the city was burned. Moscow resumed paying tribute.

lead.en: Jogaila weds Poland's queen, joining Lithuania and Poland

summary.en: Under the 1385 agreement, Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania promised to become Catholic, marry Queen Jadwiga of Poland and join Lithuania to the Polish crown. In 1386 he was crowned Władysław II, founding the Jagiellonian dynasty.

lead.en: The oldest alliance in the world still in force

summary.en: The 1386 treaty sealed the Anglo-Portuguese alliance of 1373 with the marriage of King John I to an English princess. The alliance has never been broken and is considered the oldest still in force anywhere.

lead.en: A pig is tried in court and executed dressed as a human

summary.en: Medieval Europe put animals on trial like people, with prosecution, defence and sentence. In 1386 at Falaise a sow accused of killing a child was dressed in human clothes before her execution.

title.en: Rise of the Kingdom of Kongo

lead.en: One of Central Africa's largest states takes shape

summary.en: Around 1390 the Kingdom of Kongo emerged on the lower Congo River, with its capital at Mbanza Kongo. By the time the Portuguese arrived in the 1480s it was one of the largest states in Central Africa.

lead.en: A dynasty that would rule Korea for over 500 years

summary.en: In 1392 General Yi Seong-gye overthrew the last ruler of Goryeo and founded a new dynasty, which soon named the country Joseon. Two years later the capital moved to Hanyang, today's Seoul. The state was built on Neo-Confucian lines with civil-service examinations, and lasted until 1897, with the Yi dynasty reigning until Japan's annexation in 1910.

lead.en: A royal masquerade where the "wild men" caught fire

summary.en: Charles VI and five courtiers dressed as "wild men" in costumes of linen and pitch. A torch set them ablaze; four died, and the king was saved by the Duchess of Berry, who smothered the flames with her skirts.

title.en: Timur crushes Tokhtamysh on the Terek

lead.en: A blow from which the Golden Horde never recovered

summary.en: Timur defeated his former ally Tokhtamysh, then sacked Sarai and other Horde cities and reached Yelets. Moscow braced for invasion, but Timur turned back. The defeat hastened the Golden Horde's break-up into separate khanates.

lead.en: A pavilion covered in gold leaf, built as a shogun's villa

summary.en: Shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu built a villa whose upper floors are covered in gold leaf; after his death it became a temple. In 1950 a young monk burned it down; the pavilion seen today was rebuilt in 1955.

lead.en: Edigu crushes Vytautas, ending Lithuania's hopes in the steppe

summary.en: Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania backed the deposed khan Tokhtamysh against Edigu's protégé, Khan Temür Qutlugh. On the Vorskla his army, with Rus' princes and Teutonic knights, was routed. Dozens of princes were killed, and Vytautas's plans to control the Horde collapsed.

lead.en: A port with its hand on the throat of the spice trade

summary.en: Around 1400 an exiled prince, Parameswara, founded a town on the narrow Strait of Malacca, the main sea lane between the Indian Ocean and China. Malacca quickly became Southeast Asia's greatest market, adopted Islam and spread it across the region; Zheng He's fleet called there. The Portuguese Tomé Pires wrote that whoever is lord of Malacca has his hand on the throat of Venice.

lead.en: Timur captures Sultan Bayezid and nearly ends the Ottomans

summary.en: Timur routed the army of Sultan Bayezid I the Thunderbolt and took him prisoner; Bayezid died in captivity in 1403. His sons fought each other for the throne for a decade, and the Ottoman state nearly fell apart. The defeat delayed the fall of Constantinople by half a century.

lead.en: Hundreds of Ming ships sail as far as Africa

summary.en: Admiral Zheng He's fleet of hundreds of ships made seven voyages across the Indian Ocean, reaching Arabia and the East African coast. The expeditions displayed Ming power, but the court halted them after 1433.

lead.en: The last record of the Greenland Norse is a wedding

summary.en: In September 1408 Thorstein Olafsson and Sigrid Björnsdóttir were married in the stone church at Hvalsey. It is the last written record of the Norse settlers of Greenland; within decades the colony had vanished.

lead.en: The world's largest encyclopedia until Wikipedia

summary.en: Compiled on the Yongle Emperor's orders, it ran to 22,937 chapters in 11,095 volumes. It remained the world's largest encyclopedia for almost 600 years, until Wikipedia overtook it in 2007.

lead.en: Poland and Lithuania break the might of the Teutonic Order

summary.en: On 15 July 1410 the armies of Poland and Lithuania under Jogaila and Vytautas routed the Teutonic Order. One of the largest battles of medieval Europe, it broke the Order's power in the Baltic region.

lead.en: The oldest astronomical clock still working

summary.en: The astronomical clock on the Old Town Hall was built in 1410 by clockmaker Mikuláš of Kadaň and astronomer Jan Šindel. It is the oldest such clock still working; every hour the apostles parade past its windows.

lead.en: The most famous Russian icon

summary.en: Andrei Rublev painted the Trinity for the cathedral of St Sergius's monastery, in 1411 or in 1425–1427 by different accounts. Three angels at a table, free of clutter and in luminous blues, became a model for icon painters. The icon is now in the Tretyakov Gallery.

title.en: A giraffe at the Ming court

lead.en: The Chinese court hails a giraffe as the mythical qilin

summary.en: In 1414 envoys from Bengal, sailing with Zheng He’s fleet, presented a giraffe to the Yongle Emperor. The court saw in it a qilin, the auspicious beast that appears under a wise ruler, and a court artist painted its portrait.

lead.en: Lê Lợi drives the Ming occupiers out of Đại Việt

summary.en: Ming China conquered Đại Việt in 1407. In 1418 the landowner Lê Lợi raised a revolt at Lam Sơn and waged a guerrilla war for ten years. After the Ming armies were routed at Chi Lăng in 1427, the Chinese withdrew, and Lê Lợi became emperor, founding the Later Lê dynasty.

lead.en: A 15th-century book that no one has been able to read

summary.en: Radiocarbon dating puts its vellum at 1404–1438. It is written in an unknown script and full of strange plants and bathing women; neither wartime codebreakers nor modern scholars have deciphered it.

lead.en: A palace closed to commoners for almost 500 years

summary.en: The Yongle Emperor moved the capital to Beijing and finished his palace of 980 buildings in 1420. Legend says it has 9,999 rooms, one fewer than the palace of the Lord of Heaven; in fact it has fewer.

lead.en: The best star catalogue between Ptolemy and Tycho Brahe

summary.en: Timur's grandson Ulugh Beg, ruler of Samarkand, built an observatory on Kuhak hill in the 1420s, with a giant sextant about 40 metres in radius. His astronomers compiled the Zij-i Sultani, tables giving the positions of more than a thousand stars and a length of the year within about a minute of the true value. After Ulugh Beg was murdered in 1449 the observatory was destroyed; archaeologist Vasily Vyatkin unearthed its remains in 1908.

lead.en: Three city-states launch an empire over central Mexico

summary.en: The cities of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan formed an alliance and defeated Azcapotzalco. Thus arose the Aztec Empire, which within a century dominated most of central Mexico.

lead.en: A peasant girl turns the tide of the Hundred Years' War

summary.en: Joan of Arc, a peasant girl convinced of her divine mission, led a French force that lifted the English siege of Orléans in nine days. The Dauphin Charles was soon crowned at Reims, marking the turning point of the Hundred Years' War.

lead.en: Heir to Great Zimbabwe, trading gold with Swahili and Portuguese

summary.en: By tradition, around 1430 Nyatsimba Mutota of the Great Zimbabwe state moved north and subdued the Zambezi valley. His title, mwene mutapa, 'lord of the conquered lands', became 'Monomotapa' in European mouths. The state traded gold and ivory with the Swahili towns and, from the 16th century, with the Portuguese.

lead.en: The largest brick dome ever, built without centring

summary.en: For decades Florence's cathedral rose around a vast opening that nobody knew how to roof. Brunelleschi built it without wooden centring, laying some 4 million bricks in herringbone; it is still the largest brick dome.

lead.en: Cusco grows into pre-Columbian America's largest state

summary.en: Pachacuti, ruler of Cusco, repelled the Chanka invasion and began turning a small kingdom into the empire of Tawantinsuyu. Within a century the Incas built the largest state of pre-Columbian America, with some 40,000 km of roads.

title.en: Rise of the Khanate of Kazan

lead.en: Ulugh Muhammad, ousted from the Horde, settles on the Volga

summary.en: Khan Ulugh Muhammad, driven out of the Golden Horde, established himself in Kazan in the late 1430s, on the lands of former Volga Bulgaria. The Khanate of Kazan became one of the Horde's successor states and for over a century fought Moscow or depended on it, until Ivan the Terrible took Kazan in 1552.

title.en: Oba Ewuare and the rise of Benin

lead.en: Ewuare the Great builds a kingdom famed for its bronzes

summary.en: Oba Ewuare the Great made Benin a powerful state and surrounded its capital with vast moats and earthworks. Benin's craftsmen became famous for bronze plaques and sculptures, looted by the British in 1897.

lead.en: Hacı Giray breaks Crimea away from the Horde, until 1783

summary.en: Around 1441 Hacı Giray, a descendant of Genghis Khan, became independent khan of Crimea with the backing of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. His Giray dynasty ruled for over three centuries; from 1475 the khanate was an Ottoman vassal, and in 1783 Russia annexed it.

lead.en: King Sejong sent identical rain gauges across the country

summary.en: In 1441 King Sejong had an iron rain gauge cast, and a year later identical vessels were placed in every province to plan taxes and rice planting. It was the world's first network of standard rain gauges.

lead.en: Giant birds wiped out soon after people arrive

summary.en: Giant flightless moa up to 3.6 m tall lived only in New Zealand. Polynesians arrived around 1300, and radiocarbon data suggest that by about 1445 every moa species had been hunted out, as printing was being invented in Europe.

lead.en: When the moa vanish, their giant hunter goes with them

summary.en: The largest eagle known, with a wingspan up to 3 m, preyed on moa. When the Māori wiped out its prey, it vanished too, estimated around 1445. It may live on in Māori legend as the man-eating bird pouākai.

lead.en: Grand Prince Vasily II is taken captive by the Kazan Tatars

summary.en: Near Suzdal the sons of Khan Ulugh Muhammad routed the Muscovite army and captured Grand Prince Vasily II. He was freed for a huge ransom, but in 1446 his rival Dmitry Shemyaka seized Moscow and blinded him, earning him the name Vasily the Blind. The civil war ended only in 1453.

lead.en: A simple alphabet takes literacy beyond the elite

summary.en: King Sejong the Great of Korea promulgated the Hunminjeongeum, a phonetic alphabet created under his direction in 1443. The simple Hangul script let literacy spread beyond the elite schooled in Chinese characters.

lead.en: Books go mass-market — and Europe starts reading

summary.en: In Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg developed printing with movable metal type on a press. His Bible appeared around 1455; printing made books cheap and accelerated the spread of knowledge, the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution.

lead.en: An Inca mountain retreat the Spanish never found

summary.en: High in the Andes an estate of precisely fitted stone was built for the Inca ruler Pachacuti. The Spanish never found it, and after Hiram Bingham publicised it in 1911 it became the symbol of Inca civilisation.

lead.en: Five warring nations agree to a 'Great Law of Peace'

summary.en: According to tradition, the Peacemaker Deganawida and Hiawatha persuaded the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca to end their wars and unite. Scholars date the founding variously, from the 12th to the early 17th century. A council of chiefs handled common affairs, while clan mothers chose and could depose the chiefs. The Tuscarora joined in 1722.

lead.en: Legend says an eruption split an island in two

summary.en: Oral traditions of Vanuatu tell of an island, Kuwae, destroyed by a volcanic eruption in the 15th century, leaving Epi and Tongoa behind. A submarine caldera does lie between them. Scientists long tied Kuwae to a huge sulphur spike around 1452 seen in ice cores, but that link is now disputed.

lead.en: 40,000 km of roads, built by a people without wheels or horses

summary.en: The Incas tied their empire together with roughly 40,000 km of roads, with rope bridges and way stations every few kilometres. They had no wheels or horses: the roads carried runners called chasquis and llama trains.

lead.en: The Ottomans end the thousand-year Byzantine Empire

summary.en: After a siege of nearly two months, the army of Ottoman sultan Mehmed II stormed Constantinople; the last emperor, Constantine XI, died in the fighting. Byzantium fell, the city became the Ottoman capital, and Moscow later claimed Byzantium's legacy.

lead.en: War by appointment, fought for captives rather than victory

summary.en: After the famine of the 1450s the Aztecs and their Tlaxcalan neighbours began staging prearranged battles. No land was taken: warriors tried to capture enemies alive, for prestige and for sacrifice.

lead.en: Earthworks running for thousands upon thousands of km

summary.en: For centuries ditches were dug and ramparts raised around Benin's capital and its villages. Their total length across the country is estimated at 16,000 km; Guinness lists them as the longest earthworks of the pre-mechanical era.

lead.en: Mehmed II takes the last fragment of Byzantium

summary.en: The Empire of Trebizond arose on the southern shore of the Black Sea in 1204, when the crusaders took Constantinople. Eight years after Constantinople fell, Mehmed II besieged Trebizond by land and sea, and Emperor David Megas Komnenos surrendered. It was the end of the last Greek state to succeed Byzantium.

lead.en: Kerei and Janibek lead their clans away to Zhetysu

summary.en: Kerei and Janibek, Genghisid descendants of Jochi, broke away with their people from the Uzbek khan Abu'l-Khayr and moved to Zhetysu, in the lands of Moghulistan. The breakaways came to be called Kazakhs, meaning free men. The traditional founding date of the khanate is 1465, and in 2015 Kazakhstan celebrated its 550th anniversary.

lead.en: Songhai becomes West Africa's largest empire

summary.en: The Songhai ruler Sonni Ali took Timbuktu from the Tuareg and then Djenné, making Songhai the largest empire in West Africa. Under his successor Askia Muhammad, Timbuktu became a renowned centre of Islamic learning.

lead.en: A Tver merchant reaches India 30 years before Vasco da Gama

summary.en: The Tver merchant Afanasy Nikitin sailed down the Volga, crossed Persia and around 1469 reached India, where he spent almost three years, including in Bidar, capital of the Bahmani Sultanate. He died near Smolensk on the way home; his notes, A Journey Beyond Three Seas, are one of the first European accounts of India.

lead.en: The Incas' main rival on the Peruvian coast falls

summary.en: Around 1470 Inca armies under Tupac Inca Yupanqui conquered the kingdom of Chimor and its capital Chan Chan, the largest state on the Peruvian coast. The last ruler, Minchancaman, was taken to Cusco, along with Chimor's skilled goldsmiths. The Incas became masters of almost all of Peru.

lead.en: Moscow routs Novgorod's militia; the republic's end draws near

summary.en: When Novgorod sought an alliance with Lithuania, Ivan III sent his armies against it. On the Shelon the Muscovites routed a far larger Novgorod militia. Under the Treaty of Korostyn Novgorod renounced the Lithuanian alliance, and seven years later, in 1478, it lost its independence.

lead.en: Ivan III abolishes the veche and carts off its bell

summary.en: In January 1478 Novgorod surrendered to Ivan III. Its veche assembly was abolished and the veche bell taken to Moscow. Absorbing Novgorod's vast lands was a key step towards a unified Russian state.

lead.en: A crown-run tribunal that lasted 356 years

summary.en: At the request of Ferdinand and Isabella, Pope Sixtus IV allowed them in 1478 to appoint their own inquisitors; the first auto-da-fé was held in Seville in 1481. Unlike the papal Inquisition it answered to the crown, and it was abolished only in 1834.

title.en: Great Stand on the Ugra River

lead.en: Akhmat withdraws without a fight — by tradition, the yoke ends

summary.en: The armies of Grand Prince Ivan III and Khan Akhmat of the Great Horde faced each other across the Ugra River for weeks until Akhmat withdrew without battle. The event traditionally marks the end of the Tatar yoke over Russia.

lead.en: The Silver Pavilion was never silver

summary.en: Shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa began this villa in imitation of his grandfather's Golden Pavilion. It was never covered in silver; the name "Silver Pavilion" was only coined in the Edo period, over a century later.

title.en: Building the brick walls of the Moscow Kremlin

lead.en: Italian masters build the fortress that still stands today

summary.en: In 1485–1495, under Ivan III, Italian masters including Pietro Antonio Solari built the new brick walls and towers of the Moscow Kremlin. The fortress survives to this day.

lead.en: The witch-hunters' handbook appears on the eve of modernity

summary.en: Heinrich Kramer's treatise was printed in Speyer in 1486, three decades after Gutenberg, and ran through dozens of editions. The largest witch hunts came later still, between about 1560 and 1630.

title.en: Dias rounds the Cape of Good Hope

lead.en: Proof that a sea route to India around Africa exists

summary.en: The Portuguese expedition of Bartolomeu Dias was the first European voyage to round the southern tip of Africa and enter the Indian Ocean. It proved that a sea route to India around Africa was possible.

lead.en: The Old World and the New are linked for good

summary.en: Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain in search of a western route to Asia, landed on the Bahamian island of Guanahani on 12 October 1492. It began lasting contact between the Old and New Worlds, transforming both hemispheres.

lead.en: The Reconquista ends; that same year Spain expels its Jews

summary.en: After a ten-year war, the Catholic Monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella accepted the surrender of Granada, the last Muslim state in Iberia. Its fall completed the Reconquista; the same year Spain expelled its Jews.

lead.en: A stone falls into a wheat field and survives to this day

summary.en: On 7 November 1492 a stony meteorite of about 127 kg fell in a wheat field near Ensisheim, one of the oldest falls both documented and preserved. Only weeks earlier Columbus had reached the Bahamas.

title.en: Askia Muhammad seizes power in Songhai

lead.en: A general makes Songhai one of Africa's largest empires

summary.en: In 1493 the general Muhammad Ture overthrew the son of Sonni Ali and founded the Askia dynasty. He divided the realm into provinces under appointed governors, created a standing army and standard weights. After his hajj he was named caliph of the Western Sudan in Cairo. Under him Songhai stretched from the Atlantic to the Niger and became one of the largest empires in African history.

lead.en: Spain and Portugal split a world not yet discovered

summary.en: Spain and Portugal divided the lands of the world, discovered and yet to be discovered, along a meridian 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands. That is why Brazil became Portuguese while the rest of Latin America became Spanish.

lead.en: One law for the Muscovite state, and St George's Day

summary.en: The first law code for all of Muscovy set a single procedure for courts and fees. Its best-known article limited peasants' moves between landlords to a week either side of St George's Day in autumn, a first step towards serfdom.

lead.en: Florence burns mirrors, cards, perfumes and paintings

summary.en: At the 1497 carnival, followers of the preacher Savonarola piled mirrors, cosmetics, playing cards, books and paintings in the Piazza della Signoria and burned them. A year later Savonarola himself was executed in the same square.

lead.en: Europe opens direct sea trade with Asia

summary.en: Vasco da Gama's Portuguese squadron sailed around Africa and reached Calicut on India's Malabar Coast. Opening the sea route to India launched direct European maritime trade with Asia and European colonial expansion.
